**Michael Bayer ([@zzzeek](https://github.com/zzzeek)) wrote:**

yeah, auto correlation historically was never intended to use the same `select()` in multiple correlation contexts like that, it was intended to be a typing saver vs. having to say `correlate()` explicitly.  There was no anticipation that a single `select()` would be intentionally correlating in more than one way.   That you want it to stretch out and take advantage to the JOIN, when present, is pretty unusual.

Of course just taking out the assertion solves the whole issue here, but then leaves us open to miss a pattern that is in the vast majority of cases a user error which can render as silently returning the wrong results.  Turning it into a warning is one option.

SQL-wise, you get the same results if you just correlate fixed to Document:


    class Document(Base):
        __tablename__ = 'documents'
    
        id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    
        @classmethod
        def __declare_last__(cls):
    
            cls.result_type = column_property(
                select([distinct(Result.type)](distinct(Result.type)))
                .where(Result.document_id == cls.id).correlate(cls)
            )


I guess you're just really hoping to have it implicitly "optimize" itself in a very specific JOIN scenario?  Or do you actually want different data in cls.result_type for special JOIN scenarios? (both are not how things were intended...)

**Luke Cyca ([@lukecyca](https://github.com/lukecyca)) wrote:**

You're right: I hit this issue while trying to optimize a query which joins these two tables together. Previously, I just correlated to `cls.__table__` (as you suggested) which works, but results in a slow loop when I EXPLAIN ANALYZE the joined query in Postgres. I made it fast by correlating to ''both'' tables, but then it breaks when the Result class isn't joined to the superquery.

Removing [this if block](source:/lib/sqlalchemy/sql/expression.py#L5274) is what I had in mind for fixing this issue, but I'm not surprised that it's there for a good reason. Another solution would be to support `Select.correlate('*')` which would correlate to every table that's available in the superquery but not fail when they all end up correlated.

Do you have any other suggestions? Can I optimize the specific query with some combination of query options? Am I misusing `column_property()`?

**Michael Bayer ([@zzzeek](https://github.com/zzzeek)) wrote:**

yes that's the assertion in question I was referring to.  It's there for a *reason*, though it's hard for me to accurately say it's a *good* reason, as I don't know how often users come across that error and prevents them from getting a wrong result.   If we didn't have it there, and users came to me all the time with "I'm getting the wrong result!" then we'd know.

So we have to go to the history books, and I think the argument is looking kind of weak here.  Here's what we added in 0.3.4, which is when we had an extremely small userbase:

    changeset:   1897:37a61a1b497cb44d0098d188255238ddf4e8e38c
    user:        zzzeek
    date:        Fri Jan 19 02:19:38 2007 +0000
    files:       CHANGES lib/sqlalchemy/sql.py test/sql/select.py
    description:
    
    another fix to subquery correlation so that a subquery which has only one FROM
    element will *not* correlate that single element, since at least one FROM element is
    required in a query.

I don't know if that "fix" was in response to a user issue or not, it's likely someone reported it though.  It's easy to generate the error here but it's not so clear if there's a usage pattern where correlation to everything seems like a surprise.

then in 0.4.5, backpedal, as someone needed to SELECT with all the FROMs correlated:

      Can now allow selects which correlate all FROM clauses and
      have no FROM themselves.  These are typically used in a
      scalar context, i.e. SELECT x, (SELECT x WHERE y) FROM
      table.  Requires explicit correlate() call.


So the explicit correlate() call here was a hedge on what used to be implicit, now we made the decision that a user who really wanted to correlate on everything can do so, but has to tell us that's what (s)he wants since it's a little unusual.

I tried to identify cases where your use of auto-correlation might produce a query you don't want, based on if you embedded in a SELECT against Result that's used in some other context, but I couldn't really figure one out, didn't try that hard though.

So yes we might just take that assertion out.  Maybe turn it into a warning, though overall SQLAlchemy's usual philosophy is to not second guess valid SQL, and invalid SQL will be reported by the database in any case.

**Luke Cyca ([@lukecyca](https://github.com/lukecyca)) wrote:**

I can think of a potentially surprising result of allowing all tables to correlate by default. Consider this:


    class Employee(Base):
        __tablename__ = "employees"
    
        id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
        department_id = Column(Integer, ForeignKey("departments.id"))
    
        department = relationship("Department")
    
    class Department(Base):
        __tablename__ = "departments"
    
        id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    
        employee_count = column_property(
            select([func.count('*')](func.count('*')))  # correlate=True is the default
            .where(Employee.department_id == id)
        )
        
    session = Session()
    
    
    print session.query(Department).filter_by(id=123).one().employee_count
    # Returns the number of Employees in Department id 123
    
    
    print session.query(Employee).options(joinedload(Employee.department)).filter(Employee.id == 99).one().department.employee_count
    # Actual result: 1
    # Expected result: the total number of employees in employee 99's department



Proposal:
 * Leave the assert where it is so people don't run into the situation above. auto-correlation remains unchanged.
 * Change the behaviour of explicit correlation so that it only occurs when the from is available in the superquery. This would involve changing  [this line](source:/lib/sqlalchemy/sql/expression.py#L5263) to something like:

    froms = [   f for f in froms if f not in _cloned_intersection(
            _cloned_intersection(froms, existing_froms),
            self._correlate
        )
    ](
    )


If that seems reasonable, I can take a crack at it and submit a pull request via BitBucket.

**Michael Bayer ([@zzzeek](https://github.com/zzzeek)) wrote:**

yeah, that was the other way I thought of too, and I do like that approach, that's probably how correlate()/correlate_except() should work.  But it's a more significant behavioral change.  I'm not thinking of any major surprises due to it unless someone has unit tests that are asserting a select() with correlate() on it by itself produces certain SQL.   We're right at the edge of 0.8 final and I've already run through the betas, what do you think ?   I'm inclined to go for it, if things don't obviously break within the existing tests.

**Luke Cyca ([@lukecyca](https://github.com/lukecyca)) wrote:**

OK. I'll implement it and see what breaks.

What's the deadline in order to make it into 0.8? Is BitBucket your preferred way to take a patch?

**Michael Bayer ([@zzzeek](https://github.com/zzzeek)) wrote:**

sure a pullreq on bitbucket is good.

I really would like to release 0.8 before Pycon in two weeks.

**Luke Cyca ([@lukecyca](https://github.com/lukecyca)) wrote:**

I've implemented it as discussed and committed it here: https://bitbucket.org/lukecyca/sqlalchemy. 8 tests are failing as a result, and I've gotten stuck on the very first one (and need input).


    FAIL: test.orm.test_froms.RawSelectTest.test_select
    ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    Traceback (most recent call last):
      File "/Volumes/Spinny/Users/luke/Code/sqla-env/lib/python2.7/site-packages/nose/case.py", line 197, in runTest
        self.test(*self.arg)
      File "/Volumes/Spinny/Users/luke/Code/sqla-env/sqlalchemy/test/orm/test_froms.py", line 188, in test_select
        "SELECT users.id AS users_id, users.name AS users_name, "
      File "/Volumes/Spinny/Users/luke/Code/sqla-env/sqlalchemy/./lib/sqlalchemy/testing/assertions.py", line 215, in assert_compile
        eq_(cc, result, "%r != %r on dialect %r" % (cc, result, dialect))
      File "/Volumes/Spinny/Users/luke/Code/sqla-env/sqlalchemy/./lib/sqlalchemy/testing/assertions.py", line 135, in eq_
        assert a == b, msg or "%r != %r" % (a, b)
    AssertionError: 'SELECT users.id AS users_id, users.name AS users_name, anon_1.email AS anon_1_email FROM users JOIN (SELECT addresses.id AS id, addresses.email_address AS email FROM addresses, users WHERE addresses.user_id = users.id) AS anon_1 ON anon_1.id = users.id' != 'SELECT users.id AS users_id, users.name AS users_name, anon_1.email AS anon_1_email FROM users JOIN (SELECT addresses.id AS id, addresses.email_address AS email FROM addresses WHERE addresses.user_id = users.id) AS anon_1 ON anon_1.id = users.id' on dialect <sqlalchemy.engine.default.DefaultDialect object at 0x112eac610>


I'm worried that this approach cannot support `query(...).correlate(...).alias()` because at the time the aliased query is compiled, there are no existing_froms, so the correlate() will be ineffective.

What do you think?

**Michael Bayer ([@zzzeek](https://github.com/zzzeek)) wrote:**

hm, maybe the "and len(froms) > 1" is the issue here?   the way things are moved around in https://bitbucket.org/lukecyca/sqlalchemy/commits/6f0623292e0c8603b4fb059708c38a42907fef3a suggests the logic has changed a bit.   in that test, unless I'm missing something there's only one "compile()" happening and it should only be against the fully composed statement (though I'd have to pdb through it to see exactly if this is the case).

**Luke Cyca ([@lukecyca](https://github.com/lukecyca)) wrote:**

The problem above was because `existing_froms` wasn't getting populated if the subquery was `asfrom`. I moved that logic up a level so that it gets populated in all cases (but auto-correlation remains unapplied if the subquery is `asfrom`).

A lot of the tests required changes because they would call `.correlate()` on a simple `Select` that wasn't actually in a superquery at all.

Anyway, a [pull request](https://bitbucket.org/zzzeek/sqlalchemy/pull-request/3/changed-behavior-of-selectcorrelate-to/diff) is up for your perusal. This is my first foray into SQLa internals, so I'm certainly open to criticism!

**Michael Bayer ([@zzzeek](https://github.com/zzzeek)) wrote:**

that's really great work, there are *very* few people who go into the internals at that level, and this particular code I don't think anyone has ever worked on it other than me, so very nice!   

I do want to go through the tests in test_generative, perhaps rework them from how they were before as I need to make sure the intent of those tests aren't changing, just looking at the diff it's not clear to me the original intent on some of these - these tests came from when I'd have some very involved bug reports of very complex ORM scenarios, where I'd spend sometimes multiple days distilling the mechanical issue into that series of tests.   For most of those tests, I need to spend an hour just getting my head back into the specific thing being dealt with.  A bunch of them seem to now validate SQL of the form "select * from t1, (select * from t2 where t2.foo=t1.bar)", which I think is not valid SQL (you can't correlate in the FROM clause) and it's puzzling to me that the correlation is working out that way, but that's probably how it always was.

Basically I need to fully wrap my head around the behavior to make sure it's not going to introduce any issues.   great work!

**Michael Bayer ([@zzzeek](https://github.com/zzzeek)) wrote:**

I've made some continued changes here, including a rework of the tests, as well as improved the "FROM" logic I referred to above; the correlation now does not take any effect if the SELECT is used as a FROM, as this is not valid SQL in any case.   Since `.correlate()` and `.correlate_except()` are now extensions of "auto correlation" I think this is appropriate and also an improvement.

Your change is in: 3b7fbdb2962439438c38e972843d3c8ef05eb216

I started tackling some of the tests in: 9793bf7fb26af7fced221096d2ca75a37d941001

The additional FROM change is in: d5d9a8c24ed178cbc45c7caf8452e0fda5578ea4

more test cleanup and changelog in: a5ec70a9613abdc811c132f9d8e5d76c2fb8aa6d, 9066d99a0f978c942593ca53eca9bf89a1d62d80, d2a256a3ad48341e013b6e7a3e911495e5b5d31a

Thanks for all the amazing work on this !

**Conor Davis ([@avoidscorn](https://github.com/avoidscorn)) wrote:**

This change causes problems for me, as I rely on "invalid" SELECT-used-as-a-FROM behavior. PostgreSQL at least supports it. My use case: given a parent table and child table, find the parent whose max-child satisfies some condition.

Example:

    import sqlalchemy as sa
    
    metadata = sa.MetaData()
    parent = sa.Table("parent", metadata,
        sa.Column("id", sa.Integer, primary_key=True))
    child = sa.Table("child", metadata,
        sa.Column("id", sa.Integer, primary_key=True),
        sa.Column("parent_id", sa.Integer, sa.ForeignKey("parent.id")),
        sa.Column("pos", sa.Integer))
    
    # Find the max-child for a given parent.
    child_q = sa.select([child](child))
    child_q = child_q.where(child.c.parent_id == parent.c.id)
    child_q = child_q.order_by(child.c.pos)
    child_q = child_q.limit(1)
    child_q = child_q.correlate(parent)
    child_q = child_q.alias("max_child")
    
    max_child_q = sa.select([1](1), from_obj=child_q)
    # Arbitrary max-child condition.
    max_child_q = max_child_q.where(child_q.c.id == 1)
    
    q = sa.select([parent](parent))
    q = q.where(sa.exists(max_child_q))
    print q


Produces this SQL:

    SELECT parent.id
    FROM parent
    WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1
    FROM (SELECT child.id AS id, child.parent_id AS parent_id, child.pos AS pos
    FROM child, parent
    WHERE child.parent_id = parent.id ORDER BY child.pos
     LIMIT :param_1) AS max_child
    WHERE max_child.id = :id_1)


Note the unwanted "parent" FROM clause in the innermost SELECT. It does not show up in 0.7.x.

I realize there are more efficient ways to do max-child queries, but this method is convenient when the code that generates the max-child clause is independent from the code that creates the overall query.

issue.body:
**Migrated issue, originally created by Sok Ann Yap ([@sayap](https://github.com/sayap))**

This is related to the mailing list post: https://groups.google.com/forum/?fromgroups#!topic/sqlalchemy/Ld0iuCUphHU

It seems like #2668 has universally disabled correlation for subquery inside a FROM clause. The situations where such expression is needed could be quite rare, but it is sometimes necessary to do so, especially for lesser databases such as SQL Server. An example would be this:

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/5786739/porting-postgresql-string-agg-to-sql-server-problem-with-order-by

Another example would be a subquery that returns a couple of computed values, with an outer query consists entirely of a CASE statement in its select list that makes use of the values.

(Note that these examples are used in the context of hybrid / column property)

I think it would be good to add a flag to `select()` to enforce the correlation when necessary.

----------------------------------------
